# Akashiwo

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A relatively large athecate ("naked", no armour plates) dinoflagellate that is flattened dorsoventrally, so it looks broad and leaf-like from one side and thin edge-on (taco shapped). The cingulum (girdle) is only modestly displaced, and an apical groove runs over the top of the cell. Cells lack the rigid plate pattern of armored dinoflagellates and can appear brownish from chloroplasts. Often found during mid-mitotitic division. Akashiwo sanguinea forms red tides. Key features: large size, smooth naked outline, bifricated (notched) hypocone and domed epicone.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **gyrodinium** | Both are unarmored, however Gyrodinium's cingulum is strongly displaced into an S-shaped (sigmoid), twisted girdle. |

# Asterionellopsis

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are club-shaped (clavate): one end is expanded into a heavier "foot" while the other tapers into a long, fine trailing arm. The foot poles gather at a common centre so the colony radiates outward as a star or helix if chain is long. Key features: markedly unequal cell ends with club, central attachment, star or helical colony. Asterionellopsis glacialis (most common) and Asterionellopsis kariana.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **thalassionema** | Asterionellopsis cells are clavate with a distinct foot at the colony centre. |
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros cells are more rounded and rectangular, where Asterionellopsis is agnular. Setae (if visible) radiate from both side of the valve. |

# Centric

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Centric diatoms are radially symmetric. Cells are typically disc-, drum-, cylinder-, or box-shaped. Use this class for non-chain centric cells that cannot be keyed into other labels. Key features: Circular or polygonal valve outline, often single cells from chain-forming species.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **pennate** | Pennate diatoms are elongate and bilaterally symmetric; centric diatoms are radially symmetric. |
| **thalassiosira** | Only use Thalassiosira for single cells if spine is visible, otherwise centric. |

# Ceratium

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

An armored dinoflagellate whose plates are drawn out into long, slender horns: a single apical horn and usually two antapical horns that curve upward, giving a distinctive trident silhouette. Several species in Monterey, including ~T. divaricatum~ which hasns very short horns. The marine species are now placed in the genus Tripos, but are still often refered to as Ceratium. Key features: multiple long horns, rigid armored plates, relatively large.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **dinophysis** | Dinophysis is laterally flattened with a funnel-shaped cingular list and sail-like sulcal lists, not long horns. |
| **prorocentrum** | Prorocentrum is a two-valved cell with no horns and no girdle; Ceratium has prominent apical and antapical horns. |

# Chaetoceros

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are joined valve-to-valve into chains with an space between adjacent valves (aperture). Each cell has two or more setae per valve. Setae are long, thin bristles arising from the corners of the valve that may or may not contain branches. In girdle view, cells are generally rectangula. Adjacent cells are connected through fused (touching) setae. Nearlly 400 species described. For planktivore, setae can be difficult to see, except for on a few species with coarser, almost spine like setae.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **eucampia** | Eucampia has short, blunt polar horns (not fine setae) and forms curved chains with large lens-shaped apertures. Chaetoceros setae are thin, hair-like, and usually much longer than the cell is wide. |
| **pseudo-nitzschia** | Pseudo-nitzschia is pennate, seta-less, and forms straight stepped ribbons of needle-like cells. If fine bristles project from the cells, it is not Pseudo-nitzschia. |

# Dictyocha

**Group:** Other  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A silicoflagellate: the cell contains an internal siliceous (opaline) skeleton built from a basal ring with radiating spines and struts, often looking like an open star, wheel, or basket. The living cell is a single flagellate with many small golden-brown chloroplasts around the skeleton. Dictyocha fibula and D. speculum are common. Key features: geometric open silica skeleton with spines (not a solid frustule), single cell.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **centric** | Diatoms have a solid, box-like silica frustule; Dictyocha's silica is an open latticed skeleton of a ring plus spines, not a pillbox valve. |
| **heterosigma** | Heterosigma is a naked flagellate with no silica; Dictyocha has a rigid internal silica skeleton. |

# Dinophysis

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A thecate dinoflagellate that is strongly compressed laterally, so it looks like two watch-glasses joined edge to edge (clamshell). The anterior end bears a funnel-shaped cingular list (collar), and prominent wing (or sail) sulcal lists project from the left ventral margin. Often filled with food vaccole. Key features: lateral flattening, sail-like sulcal lists.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **ceratium** | Ceratium has long apical and antapical horns; Dinophysis has no horns but conspicuous cingular and sulcal lists. |
| **prorocentrum** | Prorocentrum splits into two flat valves along a sagittal suture with an apical spine; Dinophysis has the funnel collar and sail lists. |

# Ditylum

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are elongate prisms but appear rectangular in girdle view, with a distinctive central spine emerging from the middle of each valve plus a ring of small marginal spines. Often solitary or in short chains and relatively large. Ditylum brightwellii is the common species. Key features: prismatic (polygonal cross-section) box shape, prominent central valve spine, chloroplasts are visbile.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros has thin lateral setae and clear chains with apertures; Ditylum is a box-like cell with one central spine per valve. |
| **centric** | Use Ditylum when the prismatic shape and central spine are visible; fall back to Centric when the genus is unclear. |

# Eucampia

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are elliptical in girdle view and bear two blunt, broad polar elevations ("horns") at each end of the valve. Adjacent cells are joined horn-to-horn, leaving a conspicuous large, lens-shaped (biconvex) aperture between successive cells. Chains can be long or short. Because the horns are often unequal, the whole chain curves, twists, or coils rather than running straight. Key features to key on: (1) blunt, tapering horns (batman); (2) the large apertures between cells; (3) the characteristic curved or spiral chain shape. Eucampia zodiacus is the common large curved-chain form.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros bears thin, hair-like setae (bristles) that often project well beyond the cell outline and cross between neighbours. Eucampia's projections are short, blunt horns, not fine setae, and its inter-cell apertures are large and lens-shaped. The aperature shape and size is something to key on. Chaetoceros will be much smaller. |

# Gyrodinium

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

An athecate ("naked") dinoflagellate whose defining trait is a cingulum (girdle) that is strongly displaced and often wound into an S-shape, so the two halves of the cell (epicone and hypocone) look twisted relative to each other. Key features: naked outline, cingulum displacement more than 1/3 body length, food vacuoles often present

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **akashiwo** | Akashiwo is larger and dorsoventrally flattened with only a slightly offset girdle; Gyrodinium is defined by its strongly displaced, twisted (sigmoid) cingulum. |

# Heterosigma

**Group:** Other  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A raphidophyte: a naked (wall-less) flagellate, ovoid to slightly dorsoventrally flattened, with two unequal flagella emerging from a subapical groove and numerous discoid golden-brown chloroplasts arranged around the cell periphery. It has no silica frustule, no thecal plates, and no cingulum. Heterosigma akashiwo forms ichthyotoxic red tides. Key features: naked flexible cell, two flagella, many peripheral golden chloroplasts, no skeleton or plates.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **gyrodinium** | Unarmored dinoflagellates have a distinct cingulum (girdle) encircling the cell; Heterosigma has no girdle — just two flagella from a subapical pit. |
| **dictyocha** | Dictyocha carries an internal silica skeleton; Heterosigma is entirely naked with no skeleton. |

# Margalefidinium

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

An athecate dinoflagellate which typically forms motile chains of 2, 4, or up to 8 cells. The cingulum is deeply displaced and spirals around the cell. Key features: chains of naked cells, strongly spiral girdle, chloroplast-filled cells.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **gyrodinium** | Gyrodinium is typically solitary with a single sigmoid girdle; Margalefidinium swims in chains with a spirally wound cingulum. |
| **polykrikos** | Polykrikos is a fused pseudocolony bearing nematocysts and usually lacking chloroplasts; Margalefidinium forms chains of separate photosynthetic cells. |

# Pennate

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Pennate diatoms are elongate and bilaterally (mirror) symmetrical. They can be boat, rod, needle, or wedge-shaped in valve view. Use this class for pennate cells that are not centric but cannot be keyed with confidence to one of the named pennate genera in this guide. This includes non-chain (or clipped) Pseudo-nitzschia, which cannot be easily distinguished from other single celled pennates. Key features: elongate bilateral outline, no setae.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **pseudo-nitzschia** | Label Pseudo-nitzschia when narrow needle-like cells form stepped, end-overlapping chains |

# Phaeocystis

**Group:** Other  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

The recognizable bloom form is a colony: many small cells arranged in a single layer just inside the surface of a hollow, gelatinous (mucilaginous) sphere or lobed sac, so the colony looks like a clear balloon studded with cells around its rim. Solitary flagellated cells also occur. Colonies can reach several millimetres and blooms produce conspicuous foam. Key features: transparent gelatinous colony matrix, cells arranged at the colony surface, no silica frustule or thecal plates.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **tiarina** | Tiarina (a ciliate) is a single motile cell beating cilia; Phaeocystis is a gelatinous colony of many small non-ciliated cells sharing one matrix. |
| **centric** | Diatoms have a rigid silica frustule; Phaeocystis colonies are soft gelatinous spheres with no frustule. |

# Polykrikos

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

An athecate (naked) dinoflagellate whose cells are joined into a pseudocolony (typically 2, 4, or 8 fused zooids) with multiple transverse girdles and fewer nuclei than zooids. Key features: fused multi-unit pseudocolony, several girdles per unit, food vacuoles are often visible.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **margalefidinium** | Margalefidinium forms chains of separate photosynthetic (chloroplast-filled) cells; Polykrikos is a fused pseudocolony with multiple girdles and often without chloroplasts |
| **gyrodinium** | Gyrodinium is a single naked cell with one sigmoid girdle; Polykrikos is a pseudocolony of fused zooids with several girdles. |

# Prorocentrum

**Group:** Dinoflagellates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A desmokont dinoflagellate whose theca is made of two large valves joined along a lengthwise suture, like a clam shell or shield, with __no__ cingulum or sulcus grooves. The two flagella emerge together from an apical area that often bears a small tooth or spine. Cells are oval, heart-, or teardrop-shaped in valve view. Species in Monterey Bay may be narrow (_P. gracile_) or wide (_P. micans_ etc). Key features: two-valve clam-like theca, apical tooth, absence of a girdle.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **dinophysis** | Dinophysis is also two-parted but bears a funnel cingular list and sail-like sulcal lists; Prorocentrum is a plain two-valved cell with an apical spine and no lists. |
| **ceratium** | Ceratium has long horns and an obvious girdle; Prorocentrum has neither. |
| **gyrodinium** | Gyrodinium has a distinct girdle groove that wraps aroudn teh cell. From girdle view, both can have a similar shape. |

# Pseudo-nitzschia

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are long, narrow, and lanceolate to spindle-shaped (needle-like), tapering to pointed ends. Cells associate into characteristic stepped colonies: each cell overlaps its neighbour by a short length at the pointed tips, so the chain looks like offset stacked needles rather than cells joined face-to-face. Features to key on: (1) Often high length-to-width ratio; (2) the stepped end-overlap between adjacent cells; (3) Two chloroplasts per cell, each on either side of the median transapical (middle) plane. Several species and sub-classes represented here that need to be identified either with molecular probes or SEM.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros is centric and bears setae; Pseudo-nitzschia is pennate, seta-less, and forms stepped overlapping ribbons of needle-like cells. Can become challening if cells are further away. |

# Rhizosolenia / Proboscia

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Both genera are elongate, rod- to needle-like centric diatoms, many times longer than wide, occurring singly or in straight chains. Cells are cylindrical with numerous girdle bands and an obliquely conical apex drawn out into a fine process. In Rhizosolenia the apex bears an external process with small wing-like flaps (otaria) and paired claspers that link cells; in Proboscia the apex is extended into a curved, hollow "proboscis" and the claspers/otaria are absent. They are grouped here because at annotation resolution the two are routinely hard to separate. Key features: very high length-to-width ratio, cylindrical body, single tapering apical process.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros bears thin lateral setae from the valve corners and forms obvious chains with apertures; Rhizosolenia/Proboscia is a single long cylinder with one apical process, not lateral bristles. |
| **pennate** | Pennate diatoms are bilaterally symmetric; Rhizosolenia/Proboscia are centric (radially symmetric) cylinders. |

# Skeletonema

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are small, drum- to cylinder-shaped centric diatoms joined into straight chains. Adjacent cells are connected by a ring of long strutted processes around the valve margin, leaving a characteristic open, ladder-like gap between neighbouring cells. This feature can be challenging to see in the planktivoire. Key features: chains of small cylinders, marginal ring of linking tubes, visible inter-cell gap, Two Chloroplasts per cell. Highly abundant.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **thalassiosira** | Thalassiosira cells hang from a single fine central thread and sit close together; Skeletonema cells are bridged by a ring of marginal tubes with an obvious gap. |
| **chaetoceros** | Chaetoceros links cells with thin setae, can be challening to see in Planktovoire. |

# Thalassionema

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are narrow, straight, rod- or bar-shaped with rounded to slightly swollen ends and roughly uniform width along their length. They join at their corners by small mucilage pads to form characteristic zigzag chains or radiating stellate (star) clusters. If single cell, using pennate. Key features: uniform straight bars, corner-to-corner linkage, zigzag or star colony geometry. Thalassionema nitzschioides is the common form.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **asterionellopsis** | Asterionellopsis cells are clavate (club-shaped) with one inflated foot pole and taper along their length; Thalassionema cells are near-uniform bars of even width. |
| **pseudo-nitzschia** | Pseudo-nitzschia forms stepped colonies with cells overlapping along their pointed ends, not corner-linked zigzags or stars. |
| **pennate** | Use Thalassionema when the zigzag/stellate colony form is clear; fall back to Pennate if single cell. |

# Thalassiosira

**Group:** Diatoms  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

Cells are circular in valve view and disc- to drum-shaped, with areolae in radial or fasciculate rows and a ring of marginal processes. They frequently form loose chains held together by a single thin organic thread extruded from a central process, or occur singly. Key features: circular valve, radial areolae, central-thread linkage rather than marginal tubes.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **skeletonema** | Skeletonema is bridged by a ring of long marginal tubes leaving a clear gap; Thalassiosira chains hang from one fine central thread with cells close together. |
| **centric** | Use Thalassiosira when the disc shape and central-thread chains are evident; use Centric single cells (non-chain). |

# Tiarina

**Group:** Ciliates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A fusiform (spindle- to barrel-shaped) naked ciliate — no external lorica — with an apical mouth region and many longitudinal rows of cilia (kineties) running the length of a fairly rigid pellicle, which often gives a finely striped appearance. Tiarina fusus (also written T. fusa) is the common marine planktonic form and preys actively on dinoflagellates and other protists. Key features: tapered spindle outline, lengthwise ciliary rows, a single motile cell with no shell.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **tintinnid** | Tintinnids sit inside an external lorica (shell); Tiarina is a naked spindle-shaped cell with no lorica. |
| **phaeocystis** | Phaeocystis is a gelatinous colony of many small non-ciliated cells; Tiarina is a single ciliated cell. |

# Tintinnid

**Group:** Ciliates  ·  **Optics:** high-mag, low-mag

## Defining characteristics

A loricate ciliate: the cell secretes and sits inside a lorica — a cup-, vase-, trumpet-, or tube-shaped shell that may be transparent (hyaline) or built up from agglomerated particles. The ciliate body attaches at the closed end, and a crown of oral ciliary membranelles projects from the wide open mouth when feeding. Lorica shape and ornamentation are the main field characters. Key features: distinct external lorica, oral membranelle crown, a single cell inside the shell.

## Distinguishing from similar classes

| Similar class | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| **tiarina** | Tintinnids sit inside an external lorica (shell); Tiarina and other naked ciliates have no lorica. |
| **phaeocystis** | Phaeocystis is a gelatinous colony of many cells; a tintinnid is one ciliate cell inside a firm lorica. |
